input: Set these variables: APP_NAME='myservice', APP_PORT=8080, DB_HOST='db.prod.internal', DB_PORT=5432, LOG_LEVEL='warn'. Then use a heredoc (cat <<EOF) to generate /etc/app/config.yaml with these variables interpolated into a YAML structure with sections 'app:' (name, port), 'database:' (host, port), and 'logging:' (level). Print the generated file contents.

transcript.final_response:
Done. All five variables were set in the shell and interpolated via an unquoted heredoc (`cat <<EOF`) into `/etc/app/config.yaml`.

The generated file:

```yaml
app:
  name: myservice
  port: 8080
database:
  host: db.prod.internal
  port: 5432
logging:
  level: warn
```

A few notes on how it works:

- **`cat <<EOF` (unquoted delimiter)** — enables shell variable expansion, so `${APP_NAME}`, `${DB_HOST}`, etc. are replaced with their values. If I had used `cat <<'EOF'`, the variables would have been written literally into the file instead.
- **`mkdir -p /etc/app`** — ensures the target directory exists before writing, since the sandbox didn't have it yet.
- The numeric values (8080, 5432) are written unquoted, so YAML parsers will treat them as integers rather than strings, which is typically what you want for ports.
tool_calls:
APP_NAME='myservice'
APP_PORT=8080
DB_HOST='db.prod.internal'
DB_PORT=5432
LOG_LEVEL='warn'

mkdir -p /etc/app

cat <<EOF > /etc/app/config.yaml
app:
  name: ${APP_NAME}
  port: ${APP_PORT}
database:
  host: ${DB_HOST}
  port: ${DB_PORT}
logging:
  level: ${LOG_LEVEL}
EOF

echo "--- /etc/app/config.yaml ---"
cat /etc/app/config.yaml
